Mutual
MYOO-choo-ul
a. (reciprocal; given and received in equal degree between two or more parties)
Latin mutuus, borrowed, exchanged, from mutare, to change — the same root that gives mutation and mutable. What is mutual has passed both ways, given by each to the other.

Biblical Definition

Paul's one use of the word, at the close of his introduction to the Romans, is a small but telling correction of how he might have been read. He has just said he longs to see them, that he may impart some spiritual gift to establish them — language that, left there, could sound like an apostle arriving to hand down blessing from a superior height. He immediately corrects the impression: that is, that I may be comforted together with you by the mutual faith both of you and me. The gift Paul brings is real, but the comfort he expects to receive back is just as real, and he names it before the sentence is finished.

The correction matters because it describes the actual shape of fellowship among believers who have never met. Paul, apostle to the Gentiles, writing to a church he did not found and had not yet visited, still expects to be comforted by their faith as much as they by his gift. Nothing in the passage suggests this mutuality erases the real difference between an apostle's calling and an ordinary believer's; it simply insists that the traffic runs both ways even so. A faith that only ever gives and never receives, or only ever receives and never gives, has missed something Paul was careful to name in his very first letter to a church he loved before he had ever stood in front of it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): reciprocal; interchanged; given and received; acting in return, as mutual love, mutual advantage.

expand to see more

MUTUAL, a. Reciprocal; interchanged, each acting in return or correspondence to the other; given and received.

IMPART, v.t. To grant; to bestow; to give a share or portion of something to another.

ESTABLISH, v.t. To settle firmly; to confirm; to fix or set beyond danger of overthrow or change.

COMFORT, v.t. To strengthen the mind when depressed or enfeebled; to console; to give strength and hope.

FAITH, n. Belief; the assent of the mind to the truth of what is declared by another, resting on his authority and veracity.

Key Scripture

Rom 1:11 — "For I long to see you, that I may impart unto you some spiritual gift, to the end ye may be established;"

Rom 1:12 — "That is, that I may be comforted together with you by the mutual faith both of you and me."

1Co 12:25 — "That there should be no schism in the body; but that the members should have the same care one for another."

Php 2:2 — "Fulfil ye my joy, that ye be likeminded, having the same love, being of one accord, of one mind."

Modern Corruption

Mutual is flattened into mere sameness or equality of standing, when Paul uses it precisely across a real difference of calling — an apostle and an unmet church, each expecting to be comforted by the other.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; mutual still means what Webster said, given and received on both sides. The principle worth recovering is Paul's own care in Romans 1: he does not let his real apostolic authority collapse the mutuality of faith between himself and the Romans, and he does not let the mutuality erase the real authority either. Both are true in the same two verses.

The same balance runs through his figure of the body in First Corinthians — members with genuinely different functions, none dispensable, all owing the same care one for another. Mutual comfort in the faith is not a claim that all callings are identical; it is a claim that no calling, however exalted, stands outside the ordinary traffic of giving and receiving that belongs to the whole body of Christ.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek allelon (G240), one another, the ordinary word behind reciprocal Christian duty; en allelois, the phrase underlying Paul's mutual comfort in Romans 1:12.

expand to see more

Greek allelon (G240) — one another, each other; the standing New Testament word for reciprocal duty among believers.

Greek sumparakaleo (G4837) — to comfort together with; Paul's compound verb in Romans 1:12, built from the same root as Comforter.

Greek meros (G3313) — a part, a member; the individual part owed care in 1 Corinthians 12:25.

Greek schisma (G4978) — a division, a schism; the tearing mutual care is meant to prevent.

Greek sumphonos (G4859) — sounding together, agreeing; the harmony Philippians 2:2 asks for as its shape.

Usage

"“that I may be comforted together with you by the mutual faith both of you and me” — Paul's correction of his own opening words."

"“that the members should have the same care one for another” — mutuality inside the figure of one body."

"“being of one accord, of one mind” — the shared temper mutual faith is meant to produce."
